brief: Maths Standard start (root request, 18 November 2026), methods of brief 243
purpose: Research route inputs for Claude, not a canonical route or teaching approval
syllabus: Mathematics Standard 11-12 (2024), Year 12 Standard 2 and Standard 1
identifierPolicy: Exact CMS codenames; official sourceHtml preserves mathematical layout. Year 12 entries list Standard 2 and Standard 1 codenames separately (standard2ActionIds, standard1ActionIds); syllabusActions carries both, each with its course.

officialEvidence.source: NSW Curriculum Year 12 Standard 2 and Standard 1 Ratios and rates pages, as recorded in the crosswalk (read 18 November 2026)

siteSource.note: Paths are repo paths at this commit, read from the read-only local clone C:/Users/kygs/teaching-app-fix at the same commit (not modified). SHA256 values recomputed from the clone on 18 November 2026 and match the crosswalk inventory. All five Ratios and rates lessons and Year 11 Applications of measurement lessons 10 and 12 use data-step-id sections. Lesson01 and the two Year 11 lessons label worked examples we-1 to we-3; lessons 02 to 05 number their worked examples on the page with no ids (exampleIds empty; the packs cite them as 'worked example N').

recommendations: Run r01 to r14 in outline order, after the money strand and before Trigonometry (root ruling 28). Standard 2 students take all fourteen. Standard 1 students take r01, r02, r04, r06, r09, r10, r11, r12 and r13, then go to math-s12-t01 (r03, r05, r07, r08 and r14 are Standard 2 only).

Joins: r01 opens on the cordial jug that ends i23 (Standard 2) and i18's right panel (Standard 1), as i18's Revision 1 design proposes; i23 has no design yet, so its final frame must repeat that panel. Two-route final frames (ruling 38 pattern) after r02 (to r03 or r04), r04 (to r05 or r06), r06 (to r07 or r09) and r13 (to r14 or t01). r04, r06 and r09 must open without assuming r03, r05 and r07 to r08. r14 and r13's Standard 1 panel both end on the house roof triangle for t01, which moves the roof triangle from i23's pack proposal to this strand's end.
Pace flags (gentler Standard pace): r06 at risk (suggested split r06a and r06b); r07, r10 and r12 to watch. The rest fit 6 to 9 minutes.

Outline problem: r07 and r08's syllabus points name a radial survey, but radial surveys (cibe642c8e) and the triangle area and cosine rules they need sit in Trigonometry (t06 to t10), which now runs after this strand. Proposal: r07 and r08 teach site plans, aerial photos and maps; t10 adds one radial-survey area (and a rainfall volume on it) as a callback. Root to rule.

Site findings: MS-33 to MS-40 appended to docs/production/claude-pm/site-corrections-maths-standard.md, section 7 (the lottery hook, two wrong distractor explanations, a contradictory unit rule, mismatched kettle prices, gaps for plan symbols, rate conversion and the plan, photo and radial-survey part of r07 and r08).

Money and prices (rulings 5 and 32), read 18 November 2026: electricity usage about 33 c/kWh (AER Default Market Offer 2026-27 final determination, May 2026: Ausgrid flat-rate cap 33.14 c/kWh, Endeavour 33.73, Essential 35.01; as reported by Canstar, 26 May 2026; Codex re-verifies against the AER PDF); petrol about $2.25 a litre (NRMA weekly fuel report, 9 November 2026: Sydney regular unleaded average 225.3 c/L). Shop prices in anchors are realistic NSW 2026 examples, labelled as examples. No gambling (ruling 6).

Kit needs for this strand are in docs/production/claude-pm/checks/maths-standard-kit-needs-r.md; the main new parts are a part-bar for ratios (RatioBar), a scaled plan board with a ruler (ScalePlan) and a distance-time graph driven by TripSim.
covers: math-s12-r01 to math-s12-r14 (Year 12 Ratios and rates, Standard 2 and Standard 1)

entries.startBoundary: Opens on the money strand's last frame: i23 (Standard 2) and the right panel of i18 (Standard 1) both end on the water jug with a darker cordial layer and the chip "how much of the jug is cordial?". Same picture for both courses.
entries.stopBoundary: A ratio compares quantities in the same unit (a:b, order matters); a fraction compares a part with the whole, so in a:b the first part is a/(a + b) of the whole; equivalent ratios and simplest form by dividing every term by the HCF; the ratio of two quantities after converting to one unit (250 g : 1 kg = 1 : 4). Dividing a quantity in a ratio is r02.
entries.recommendation: Join: the cordial jug (250 mL cordial to 1 L water = 1 : 4, cordial is 1/5 of the jug). Keep the site's 18:24, 250 g : 1 kg and 84 cm : 1.4 m numbers. Teach the two fraction questions apart: part of the whole (3/7) and one part compared with the other (3/4). The site's lottery hook is not used (ruling 6; MS-33). Standard 1 and Standard 2 wording identical.

entries.stopBoundary: Divide a quantity in a ratio with two or three terms: count the parts, find one part, multiply out, check the shares add to the total; problems that give one share instead of the total (12 kg of sand is 3 parts); order of the terms; units on the answer; scaling a recipe up or down by the same factor. Two-route final frame: Standard 2 to r03, Standard 1 to r04.
entries.recommendation: Replace the site's $480 lottery prize with the same numbers in a non-gambling context (two cousins put in $50 and $30 for cold drinks to sell at a junior footy carnival and take $480; ruling 6, MS-33). entries.mainLearnerQuestion: How does capture-recapture estimate a population we cannot count?

syllabusActions.text: Solve practical ratio problems involving the capture-recapture technique
syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Solve practical ratio problems involving the capture-recapture technique

entryKnowledge.text: cie93c27e5: a ratio as a fraction (marked out of caught).
cid7c41f39: solving a practical ratio problem.

entries.startBoundary: r02's two-route frame; Standard 2 continues here. Nobody can count every fish in a lake.
entries.stopBoundary: Capture-recapture as two equal fractions, m2/n2 = n1/N (the share marked in the second catch matches the share marked in the whole lake), solved for N ≈ n1 × n2 / m2; the estimate is a whole number of animals; the assumptions (marked animals mix back evenly, marking does not change the chance of capture, no births, deaths or movement between catches) and which way the estimate moves when one fails. Final frame hands to r04 and must not be assumed by r04 (Standard 1 skips this video).
entries.recommendation: Standard 2 only. Lead with the fishing-lake survey (the site's 40, 50, 8 gives 250). Science-adjacent by nature: frame it as a fishing club or council survey, not a biology lesson. Keep the possum (720) and koala (300) numbers for practice only if a second example is needed.

entries.startBoundary: Opens on r03's final frame for Standard 2 and works for Standard 1 arriving from r02: a bushwalking map with a 1 : 25 000 scale in the corner and a track traced in red. The frame needs no capture-recapture knowledge.
entries.stopBoundary: A map scale 1 : n is a ratio with no units (1 of anything on the map stands for n of the same thing on the ground); map to real by multiplying by n, real to map by dividing, convert units last; a scale bar and finding n from a measured pair (n = real ÷ map in the same unit); using the real distance in a travel-time problem. Area scale factor n² is an optional one-line note, not taught.
entries.recommendation: Keep the site's 6.4 cm at 1 : 50 000 = 3.2 km, 8 cm at 1 : 25 000 = 2 km and 7.5 cm at 1 : 100 000 = 7.5 km (with the 25-minute ride). Two-route final frame: Standard 2 to r05 (construct a drawing), Standard 1 to r06 (plans).

entries.stopBoundary: Choose a scale: divide each real length by the space available, take the larger factor, round up to a friendly scale (rounding up still fits); convert every real length with the same factor and rule it; label plan and real lengths; the same drawing in a digital tool (set the scale, type real sizes) as a check. entries.mainLearnerQuestion: How does the trapezoidal rule find an area of land from a plan, photo or survey?

syllabusActions.text: Calculate the perimeter, or area of a section of land using the Trapezoidal rule where appropriate, from a site plan, an aerial photograph, a radial survey or a map that includes a scale
syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Calculate the perimeter, or area of a section of land using the Trapezoidal rule where appropriate, from a site plan, an aerial photograph, a radial survey or a map that includes a scale
syllabusActions.siteGap: Only the area by the trapezoidal rule from given offsets is taught. No perimeter, no site plan or aerial photograph with a scale, no map; radial surveys are a Trigonometry point (cibe642c8e, math-s12-t10) taught after this strand (MS-37).

entryKnowledge.text: ci3786e651: the trapezoidal rule A ≈ (h/2)(d_f + d_l), up to four applications.
ci05a36ac3: perimeters and areas of irregular blocks by dissection.
ci58f841f3: map or plan length × n = real length.

entries.startBoundary: r06's two-route frame; Standard 2 continues here. A real block of land has a creek for a back fence: no formula fits it.
entries.stopBoundary: Recall the trapezoidal rule from Year 11 in one step (one application, the site's 112 m²) and the repeated form (ends once, middles twice: 150 m², 1170 m²); new here: take the offsets and strip width from a site plan, an aerial photograph or a map with a scale, scale them to real lengths first, then apply the rule; the perimeter of the straight boundaries from the plan (fencing); why the answer is an estimate and how more offsets help. Radial surveys are named and deferred to math-s12-t10.
entries.recommendation: Outline problem: a radial survey needs triangle areas and the cosine rule (Trigonometry, math-s12-t06 to t10), which ruling 28 places after this strand; teach site plan, aerial photo and map here and give the radial-survey case to t10 (MS-37). Spoken subscripts as ruling 36 ('d f, the first offset'). Pace: watch (fits if the Year 11 rule is recalled, not re-taught).

syllabusActions.siteGap: Covered for a rectangle roof and a trapezoidal paddock; the area never comes from a scaled plan, photo or map, and the site writes V = A x d (with h used for the strip width), not the syllabus V = Ah (MS-37).

entryKnowledge.text: cie48a6b84: an area estimated from a scaled plan or photo.

entries.startBoundary: r07 ends on the farm dam's estimated area. Rainfall is reported as a depth: what does 25 mm on a roof actually give?
entries.stopBoundary: Rain as a very flat box: V = Ah with A the area in m² and h the depth converted from mm to m; m³ to litres; areas from a rectangle, a scaled plan or the trapezoidal rule (then the volume is an estimate too); tank capacity and overflow questions. entries.recommendation: Use the syllabus letters V = Ah (h is the depth of rain here, not the strip width of r07; say so once). Keep the site's 2400 L roof and 5000 L tank overflow (1480 L). Pace: fits.

entries.startBoundary: Opens on r08's final frame for Standard 2 and works for Standard 1 arriving from r06: two pay slips side by side, $336 for 8 hours and $270 for 6 hours, "who is paid more?". No r07 or r08 knowledge assumed.
entries.stopBoundary: A rate compares quantities with different units (dollars per hour, litres per minute, goals per game); a ratio compares the same unit and has no units; a unit rate is the amount for one of the second unit, found by division; comparing rates fairly by bringing both to the same unit rate. Best buys (r11), conversions (r10), speed graphs (r12) and fuel (r13) come later.
entries.recommendation: Keep the site's $336 for 8 h ($42/h) against $270 for 6 h ($45/h), the 420 pages in 7 minutes and 15 L/min. Lesson01 has no ratio-against-rate contrast beyond its definition; lesson02's key term supplies the ratio half. Pace: fits.

syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Interpret and analyse distance–time graphs to solve problems related to speed, distance and time

entries.startBoundary: Opens on r11's final frame: a road-trip receipt card, "Sydney to Melbourne, 880 km". A journey can be drawn.
entries.stopBoundary: Read a distance-time graph: distance from the start up the side, time along the bottom; a steeper line is faster; the gradient is the speed (rise in km over run in h); a flat section is a stop; a line coming down is the return trip; average speed = total distance ÷ total time (not the mean of the speeds); two journeys on one graph and where they cross (one catches the other). Draw the site's Sydney-Melbourne trip (4 h at 100 km/h, 45-minute stop, 5 h 20 min at 90 km/h: 10 h 5 min).
entries.recommendation: Site gap (crosswalk partial): the site has no graphs; original teaching from the syllabus with the site's SA 4 trip as the worked example. Pace flag: watch; suggested split only if long: r12a (reading one journey) and r12b (average speed and two journeys). TripSim (rig.tsx) can drive the car and the graph from one trip state.

entries.startBoundary: r12 ends with the Sydney-Melbourne car on the graph and a fuel gauge chip: "how much fuel did that take?".
entries.stopBoundary: Fuel consumption in L/100 km (litres used for every 100 km, a lower number is more efficient); fuel used = consumption × distance ÷ 100; cost = litres × price per litre; find consumption from a fill-up (litres ÷ km × 100); range on a full tank; compare two vehicles over the same distance in litres and dollars. Two-route final frame: Standard 2 to r14, Standard 1 to math-s12-t01.

entries.mainLearnerQuestion: How do watts, kilowatts and kilowatt hours set the cost of running an appliance?

syllabusActions.text: Recognise and convert between watts (W) and kilowatts (kW) using 1000 W = 1 kW
syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Recognise and convert between watts (W) and kilowatts (kW) using 1000 W=1 kW

syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Apply units of energy to calculate kilowatt hours and solve problems involving the consumption of energy

entryKnowledge.text: cib0e451ed: converting a rate's units (minutes to hours).
ci26fe7fac: price per unit (cents per kWh).
ci7526e53a: the prefix kilo- = 1000.

entries.startBoundary: r13's two-route frame; Standard 2 continues here. A phone on its charger and a heater plug into the same power point: which costs more to run?
entries.stopBoundary: Watts measure how fast an appliance uses energy; 1000 W = 1 kW; energy in kilowatt hours = kW × hours; cost = kWh × price per kWh; days and hours per day; comparing appliances (a lower-power appliance on for longer can cost more); reading the usage price from a bill. Prices: about 33 c per kWh (AER Default Market Offer 2026-27, Ausgrid residential flat-rate usage cap 33.14 c/kWh); say once that prices change and differ by retailer. Final frame hands to math-s12-t01.
entries.recommendation: Keep the site's 2400 W heater for 5 h at $0.32 ($3.84), the ten 60 W bulbs ($1.44) and the two-heater comparison (12 against 12.6 kWh a day). Final frame: the house with rooftop solar, its roof drawn as a right-angled triangle (35 degrees at the eave, '?' on the height), chip 'Next: right-angled triangles', so t01 opens on the same picture as r13's Standard 1 panel. Pace: fits.
